questions.q: What does Kubernetes RBAC actually decide once a request has already been authenticated?
options: Whether that already-identified subject is allowed to perform the specific action it's requesting
Which TLS certificate authority is trusted to sign client certificates
Which container image registry a Pod is allowed to pull from
How many replicas a Deployment is allowed to scale to
questions.explain: Authentication answers 'who are you?'; RBAC (authorization) answers 'is this identity allowed to do this specific thing?' RBAC is additive-only, so an unmatched request is denied by default.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?
options: A ClusterRole can only be bound to a ServiceAccount, never to a User or Group
A Role can grant delete permissions while a ClusterRole is always read-only
A Role is scoped to a single namespace; a ClusterRole is cluster-scoped or reusable across namespaces
There is no difference — ClusterRole is just the newer name for Role
questions.explain: A Role's rules only ever apply inside the namespace it's created in. A ClusterRole has no namespace, used for cluster-scoped resources like nodes or as a reusable rule set bound per-namespace.

questions.q: A ClusterRole named `node-viewer` is bound using a RoleBinding created in the `payments` namespace instead of a ClusterRoleBinding. What happens?
options: The RoleBinding is rejected outright because ClusterRoles cannot be referenced by a RoleBinding
The grant applies only within the `payments` namespace, even though the ClusterRole's rules could otherwise apply cluster-wide
The grant silently becomes cluster-wide, identical to using a ClusterRoleBinding
The grant applies to every namespace except `payments`
questions.explain: A RoleBinding can reference a ClusterRole, but doing so scopes that ClusterRole's rules down to the RoleBinding's own namespace — a common pattern for reusing one rule set across many namespaces without granting cluster-wide access.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend giving each workload its own dedicated ServiceAccount instead of letting every Pod use a namespace's `default` ServiceAccount?
options: The `default` ServiceAccount is deleted automatically after 24 hours
Pods using `default` cannot mount a volume
Sharing `default` across every workload makes it impossible to tell which app did what, or to scope permissions per-workload
Kubernetes only allows one Pod per namespace to use the `default` ServiceAccount
questions.explain: Every Pod that doesn't name a ServiceAccount uses `default` automatically. A cluster full of workloads sharing one identity makes per-workload least-privilege and auditing impossible.

questions.q: Since Kubernetes 1.22, how do ServiceAccount tokens mounted into a Pod differ from the older long-lived tokens stored in a Secret?
options: They are issued by the TokenRequest API: short-lived, audience-bound to the API server, and auto-rotated
They are no longer required for a Pod to call the API server at all
They are identical in behavior, only the file path where they're mounted changed
They can only be used from outside the cluster, never by a Pod itself
questions.explain: The correct behavior is the TokenRequest API default: short-lived, audience-bound, auto-rotated tokens — a real security improvement over the old long-lived Secret-backed tokens that never expired.
